concepts.title: What Makes a Nucleus Radioactive?
concepts.contentHtml:
A nucleus is stable when the strong force binding nucleons exactly balances electrostatic repulsion between protons. Stray too far from the 'valley of stability' (the right N/Z ratio for a given A) and the nucleus becomes radioactive — it spontaneously rearranges by emitting particles or photons.

Light stable nuclei have N ≈ Z. Heavier stable nuclei need more neutrons (N > Z) to dilute proton repulsion. Beyond Z ≈ 83 (bismuth), no nucleus is truly stable.

concepts.title: Decay Modes
concepts.contentHtml:
Different instabilities favor different decays:

• Alpha (α): emits ⁴He nucleus. Common in heavy nuclei.
• Beta-minus (β⁻): neutron → proton + e⁻ + ν̄. Common in neutron-rich nuclei.
• Beta-plus (β⁺) / electron capture: proton → neutron + e⁺ + ν. Common in proton-rich nuclei.
• Gamma (γ): deexcitation; nucleus stays the same.

Each decay shifts the nucleus toward stability. Heavy radioactive isotopes typically chain through several decays before reaching a stable end product.

concepts.title: Decay Kinetics & Half-Life
concepts.contentHtml:
Each radioactive nucleus has a probability per unit time of decaying. With many nuclei, the sample obeys N(t) = N₀ e^(−λt), with half-life t_½ = ln 2 / λ.

Half-lives span enormous ranges: ⁸Be ≈ 10⁻¹⁶ s, ²³⁸U ≈ 4.5 × 10⁹ years. Same nuclear physics, different shell structures and decay channels.

The 'rule of thumb' for radiotoxicity: an isotope's hazard is roughly inversely proportional to half-life and the energy of its emissions. Long half-life means low specific activity, but persistence; short half-life is intense but transient.

concepts.title: Carbon-14 Dating
concepts.contentHtml:
Cosmic rays hit nitrogen-14 in the upper atmosphere, producing ¹⁴C at a roughly constant rate. Living organisms exchange carbon with the atmosphere, so they have the same ¹⁴C/¹²C ratio.

When an organism dies, exchange stops. ¹⁴C decays with t_½ ≈ 5730 years. Measure the surviving ¹⁴C/¹²C ratio and you get a date.

Useful for organic samples up to ~50,000 years (eight half-lives — beyond that, the signal drops below natural variation). Has revolutionized archaeology since Libby's 1950s development (Nobel 1960).

concepts.title: Geological Dating
concepts.contentHtml:
For deeper time, longer-lived isotopes are used:

• U-Pb: zircon crystals trap U but reject Pb during growth. ²³⁸U → ²⁰⁶Pb (t_½ = 4.5 × 10⁹ y) and ²³⁵U → ²⁰⁷Pb (t_½ = 7 × 10⁸ y) give two independent clocks. Used to date the oldest rocks (4.4 billion years) and the age of Earth (4.54 billion years).
• K-Ar: ⁴⁰K → ⁴⁰Ar with 1.25 × 10⁹ y half-life. Used for volcanic rocks, including dating early hominid fossils.
• Rb-Sr: igneous and metamorphic rocks.

concepts.title: Calibration & Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
Atmospheric ¹⁴C levels actually fluctuate (cosmic ray variation, fossil-fuel burning, atomic bomb testing). Tree-ring chronologies and varved sediments calibrate raw radiocarbon dates to calendar years.

Dating depends on key assumptions: the sample remained closed (no element exchange after formation) and initial isotope ratios are known or estimable. When these fail, dates are wrong — sometimes spectacularly.

Modern accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) measures ¹⁴C atoms one by one rather than detecting their decays — letting tiny samples (mg) be dated.

concepts.title: Isotopic Tracers in Biology
concepts.contentHtml:
Mark a specific atom in a molecule with a radioactive (or stable but rare) isotope and follow it through a metabolic pathway. ¹⁴C-glucose was used to map glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. ³²P-labeled DNA helped solve the genetic code.

Tracers are exquisitely sensitive — picomole quantities are detectable. They reveal mechanism rather than just steady-state.

Stable-isotope tracers (¹³C, ¹⁵N, ²H) avoid radioactivity and are now standard in metabolic flux analysis.

concepts.title: Medical Imaging
concepts.contentHtml:
Nuclear medicine uses radiotracers to image function (not just anatomy).

PET (positron emission tomography): ¹⁸F-FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose) is taken up by metabolically active cells; positron-electron annihilation gives back-to-back gamma rays detected in coincidence. Cancer, brain activity, heart function — all imaged routinely.

SPECT: uses gamma-emitting isotopes (⁹⁹ᵐTc most commonly) and rotating cameras. Less expensive than PET, used for many diagnostics.

concepts.title: Industrial Tracers
concepts.contentHtml:
Nuclear tracers find leaks in pipelines, measure flow rates in oil refineries, and check the integrity of welds. Tiny amounts of radioactive tracer added to a process stream allow non-invasive measurement of flow patterns and residence times.

In hydrology, tritium (³H) and oxygen-18 (¹⁸O) trace groundwater age and origins. ¹⁴C in groundwater dates aquifer recharge.

The breadth is striking — from medical diagnostics to oil pipeline integrity, the same physics of isotopic labeling.

concepts.title: Nuclear Reaction Notation
concepts.contentHtml:
Nuclear reactions are typically written: target(projectile, ejectile)product. Example: ¹⁴N(α, p)¹⁷O — nitrogen-14 hit by an alpha particle ejects a proton, leaving oxygen-17. (Rutherford's first artificial transmutation, 1919.)

Conservation of mass-number, charge, energy, and momentum applies. Cross sections (probabilities, in barns: 1 barn = 10⁻²⁴ cm²) tell you how often a given reaction happens at a given energy.

concepts.title: Synthesizing Heavy Elements
concepts.contentHtml:
Elements heavier than uranium are not naturally abundant. They were made in nuclear reactors and accelerators starting in the 1940s. Plutonium, americium, californium — all from neutron capture on uranium and beyond.

The heaviest synthetic elements (oganesson, Z = 118) are made by colliding heavy-ion projectiles with heavy targets — single atoms detected before they decay in microseconds.

The hypothesized 'island of stability' near Z ≈ 114-126 may host longer-lived superheavy isotopes; experiments at GSI, RIKEN, and Dubna keep pushing toward it.

concepts.title: Activation Analysis
concepts.contentHtml:
Bombard a sample with neutrons, then look for the gamma signatures of the resulting radioactive isotopes. Neutron activation analysis (NAA) can identify trace elements down to parts per billion.

Used to authenticate art (lead and zinc isotopes in paintings), to study moon rocks, and forensically to date documents and artifacts. Non-destructive — the sample emerges intact (and slightly radioactive).

concepts.title: Reactor Fuel Chemistry
concepts.contentHtml:
Most reactors use uranium dioxide pellets enriched to a few percent ²³⁵U. Fuel rods are zirconium-clad bundles — zirconium has low neutron absorption.

Spent fuel contains fission products (Cs-137, Sr-90, I-131…), plutonium and minor actinides bred from neutron capture, and unburnt uranium. Recycling (reprocessing) extracts useful elements; once-through cycles dispose of everything.

concepts.title: Reprocessing & Plutonium
concepts.contentHtml:
The PUREX process (plutonium-uranium redox extraction) dissolves spent fuel in nitric acid, then uses tributyl phosphate to selectively extract U and Pu from fission products.

This recovers ~96% of the uranium and ~1% plutonium. Recycled into MOX (mixed oxide) fuel. France, Russia, Japan, and the UK reprocess; the US largely doesn't, citing proliferation concerns.

Newer flowsheets (UREX+, GANEX) try to keep plutonium in admixture with other actinides — making it less attractive as a weapons feedstock.

concepts.title: Waste Disposal
concepts.contentHtml:
High-level nuclear waste contains long-lived isotopes — Pu-239 (~24,000 y), Np-237 (~2 × 10⁶ y), I-129 (~1.6 × 10⁷ y). The waste must be isolated for tens of thousands to millions of years.

The international consensus is deep geological repositories: vitrified waste in stainless steel containers, buried deep in stable rock. Finland's Onkalo facility (in operation as of 2025) is the first.

Politics has been slower than chemistry. Yucca Mountain (US) was canceled. Most countries still warehouse waste in temporary surface storage.
